title: Modals in the Past and Their Perfect Forms
summary: Perfect modal forms for regret, wasted effort, unrealised possibility and arrangements in the past that were never kept.

sections.heading: Should Have Done: Criticism and Regret
sections.body:
**Should have** + past participle says that the right course of action was not taken. Turned on oneself it is regret; turned on someone else it is criticism. **Shouldn't have** + past participle is its mirror image: the action was taken, and it was a mistake. `Ought to have` carries the same meaning in a more formal register.

The same form also expresses an expectation that has not been met, with no blame attached at all — `The parcel should have arrived by Tuesday` simply reports that it has not. Only the context separates the two readings.

examples.right: I should have cited the 2019 replication study.
examples.wrong: I should cite the 2019 replication study.
examples.note: Once the essay has been submitted, regret about the omission requires the perfect form.

examples.right: They shouldn't have released the figures before the audit closed.
examples.note: The release happened and is being criticised.

examples.right: The equipment should have arrived by Tuesday, but the depot has no record of it.
examples.note: An unmet expectation rather than a reproach.

sections.heading: Needn't Have Done Versus Didn't Need To Do
sections.body:
This is the sharpest distinction in the whole area, and it is tested precisely because the two forms look interchangeable and are not.

**Needn't have** + past participle states that the action was carried out and that it turned out to be unnecessary: the effort was wasted. **Didn't need to** + infinitive states only that there was no necessity; in most contexts it implies that the action was therefore never performed, and it never asserts that it was. `Didn't have to` behaves like `didn't need to`.

examples.right: We needn't have booked a taxi — the college was running a shuttle.
examples.wrong: We needn't book a taxi — the college was running a shuttle.
examples.note: An action that was performed and proved pointless needs `needn't have` plus the past participle.

examples.right: I didn't need to renew my visa, so I saved the fee.
examples.wrong: I needn't have renewed my visa, so I saved the fee.
examples.note: `Needn't have renewed` asserts that the renewal took place, which contradicts saving the fee.

examples.right: She needn't have apologised; nobody had even noticed the error.
examples.note: The apology was made, and the second clause explains why it was wasted.

sections.heading: Could Have Done: Unrealised Possibility and Reproach
sections.body:
**Could have** + past participle most often describes something that was possible but did not happen, and in that use it can never report an achievement: an outcome actually brought off is `was able to` or `managed to`. (The same string has a second, quite separate use — the guess about a finished event, as in `She could have missed the train` — and only the context tells the two apart.)

A second use follows naturally from the first. `You could have told me` reproaches someone for not doing what was open to them; `might have` does the same work with a slightly more indignant edge.

examples.right: The fire could have spread to the neighbouring block.
examples.note: It was possible, and it did not happen.

examples.right: You could have warned me that the session had been moved.
examples.note: A reproach: the warning was open to the hearer and was not given.

examples.right: With better funding they could have completed the survey.
examples.wrong: With better funding they were able to complete the survey.
examples.note: `Were able to` reports a survey that was actually finished, which is the opposite of what is meant.

sections.heading: Would Have Done: Third Conditionals and Hypothetical Comment
sections.body:
**Would have** + past participle supplies the result clause of a third conditional, where the condition clause takes the past perfect. Keeping `would have` out of the `if` clause is one of the most valuable habits in this area, because the error is conspicuous and frequent.

The same form also softens an opinion into a hypothetical comment: `I would have thought`, `I'd have expected`. Here nothing is being reported about the past at all; the perfect form simply makes the remark more tentative.

examples.right: If the sensors had been recalibrated, the error would not have appeared.
examples.wrong: If the sensors would have been recalibrated, the error would not have appeared.
examples.note: The `if` clause takes the past perfect; `would have` belongs only in the result.

examples.right: I would have thought the deadline was in June.
examples.note: A softened opinion about the present, not a report of a past thought.

examples.right: She would have finished by now if the software had not crashed.
examples.note: A mixed conditional: a past condition with a present result.

sections.heading: Was Supposed To and Was To Have Done
sections.body:
**Was** or **were supposed to** + infinitive reports an arrangement, an instruction or a general expectation, and usually carries the implication that it was not honoured. `Was meant to` is a close informal equivalent. The `to` is part of the fixed phrase and is never dropped.

**Was** or **were to have** + past participle is the more formal counterpart, and it states outright that a planned event did not take place. `Was to` + infinitive without the perfect simply narrates a future arrangement from a past vantage point, and leaves the outcome open.

examples.right: The committee was supposed to report in March, but nothing has appeared.
examples.note: An expectation that has clearly not been met.

examples.right: The minister was to have opened the centre, but her flight was cancelled.
examples.note: `Was to have` + past participle makes the non-occurrence explicit.

examples.right: We were supposed to submit two hard copies, not one.
examples.wrong: We were supposed submit two hard copies, not one.
examples.note: `Supposed to` keeps its `to` before the infinitive.

sections.heading: Should've in Speech, Should Have in Writing
sections.body:
In connected speech the auxiliary `have` reduces to an unstressed /əv/, so `should have`, `could have`, `would have` and `must have` sound identical to `should of` and its companions. The contractions `should've` and `could've` are the accurate written record of that sound.

The spellings `should of`, `could of`, `would of` and `must of` are not. `Of` is a preposition and cannot take a participle, so the error is immediately visible on the page and is treated as a serious one. In academic writing the safest policy is to write the auxiliary out in full and leave even the legitimate contractions to speech.

examples.right: They should have checked the reference list before submission.
examples.wrong: They should of checked the reference list before submission.
examples.note: `Of` cannot govern a participle; the auxiliary is `have`.

examples.right: It must have been an administrative oversight.
examples.wrong: It must of been an administrative oversight.
examples.note: The same mishearing, with the same consequence in writing.

examples.right: We could've finished a day sooner.
examples.note: `Could've` is fine in speech and informal writing, but an essay spells it out.

slips: Writing `should of`, `could of`, `would of` or `must of`. The auxiliary is always `have`, however it sounds.
Writing `If I would have known`. The `if` clause of a third conditional takes `had known`; `would have` appears only in the result clause.
Using `should do` where the action is already finished. Regret and criticism about the past take `should have done`.
Using `didn't need to` for an action that was actually carried out and proved pointless. That is `needn't have done`.
Dropping the `to` in `was supposed to`. The phrase is fixed: `was supposed to submit`, never `was supposed submit`.
Using `could have done` for something that really happened. A realised achievement is `was able to` or `managed to`.

questions.prompt: As it turned out, she ___ have brought her passport; a driving licence was accepted as proof of identity.
questions.explain: The passport was brought and bringing it proved unnecessary, which is exactly what `needn't have` reports. `Shouldn't have` would turn a wasted precaution into a mistake.

questions.prompt: The lecture was cancelled the day before, so in the end I ___ prepare a handout at all.
questions.hint: need (there was no necessity, and the work was never done)
questions.explain: The bare infinitive `prepare` after the gap rules out `needn't have`, and the meaning is the absence of necessity rather than effort already wasted.

questions.prompt: If the committee ___ the risks earlier, the project would not have been suspended.
questions.explain: In a third conditional the `if` clause takes the past perfect and `would have` is reserved for the result clause.

questions.prompt: Looking back, we ___ the pilot study before committing to a national rollout.
questions.explain: `Looking back` places the decision in the past, and regret about a finished decision requires `should have` plus the past participle.

questions.prompt: You ___ told me the seminar had moved; I stood outside the wrong building for twenty minutes.
questions.hint: could (reproach - it was open to the hearer and was not done)
questions.explain: `Could have` and `might have` plus a past participle reproach someone for not doing what was perfectly possible at the time.

questions.prompt: The results ___ published in June, but the journal postponed the whole issue.
questions.explain: An arrangement that was not honoured is reported with `was/were supposed to`, and the phrase keeps its `to` before the passive infinitive.

questions.prompt: The authors ___ acknowledged the earlier trial in their literature review.
questions.hint: should (criticism) - write the auxiliary out in full
questions.explain: Criticism of something not done in the past takes `should have` plus the past participle, and in writing the auxiliary is spelled `have`, never `of`.

questions.prompt: I ___ thought a sample of forty was too small to support a claim that strong.
questions.explain: `I would have thought` softens an opinion held now. `Must have thought` and `should have thought` refer to an actual past thought or criticise its absence.

questions.prompt: Although the alarm system failed, the staff ___ evacuate the building in under four minutes.
questions.explain: The evacuation actually happened, so it takes `were able to`; `could` would report a general capability rather than a single success, and `could have` and `would have` cannot be followed by a bare infinitive at all.

questions.prompt: If the data had been backed up properly, the team ___ lost three months of work.
questions.hint: would (negative, result clause of a third conditional)
questions.explain: The result clause of a third conditional is `would (not) have` plus the past participle, while the condition clause carries the past perfect.

questions.prompt: She ___ the raw data before the paper had been accepted; the reviewers later asked to see it.
questions.explain: The deletion happened and is being criticised as a mistake, which is `shouldn't have`. `Needn't have deleted` would call it merely unnecessary.

questions.prompt: We ___ to submit two hard copies, but the office accepted a single file in the end.
questions.explain: `Were supposed to` reports an instruction given beforehand, typically one that events then overtook.
